newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia economy set to grow, central banker says.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia economy set to grow, central banker says.

text.p: Ethiopia's chief banker said on Thursday economic reforms and an influx of foreign aid since civil war ended in 1991 had helped turn around the country's economy.
Dubale Jale, governor of the central National Bank of Ethiopia, said far-reaching reforms including liberal financial policies since 1992 created a favourable climate for economic growth.
"Decrease in the country's previously huge defence expenses, vast amounts of foreign aid and strict fiscal policy made a significant contribution in making funds available," he said.
In a report to parliament, he said the central bank was studying correlations between the formal and informal sectors, or black market, to help speed Ethiopia's economic development.
Seventeen years of Marxist military rule almost brought the country's economy to its knees until the overthrow of dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam in 1991.
Dubale said ways for banks to give credit to peasant farmers to buy fertilisers and other inputs were also under study. Peasants provide the bulk of food for Ethiopia's 57 million people.

He said in the next three years new market instruments would be launched and the government planned to try to normalise a tight balance of payments position by such measures as sales of treasury bills.
Dubale said Ethiopia sold $1.9 billion at weekly currency auctions over the past five years to finance essential imports and 58.9 percent of these funds were used by the private sector.
The Ethiopian birr tumbled to its lowest ever level against the dollar on Monday when it was posted at 6.6530 from 6.5870 on Friday. On the black market, the birr traded at 7.15 to the dollar.
Most of the $1.9 billion came from loans and grants from international financial institutions, banking sources said.
Funds dispersed through the weekly auctions did not include $347 million which Ethiopia spends annually for imports of petroleum products, fertilisers and pharmaceuticals, they added.

Dubale said that Ethiopia had also allowed six private insurance companies with an aggregate capital of $10.6 million and three private banks with a total paid up capital of around $7.9 million to operate as part of its economic reforms.
A state-owned insurance firm with a capital of $9.2 million and three government-owned commercial banks with aggregate capital of $92.2 million were also operational, he said.
A cut in interest rates charged by commerical banks on loans to 10.5 percent from 16 percent, reduction in import tariffs and reforms in tax policies had also helped in plans for growth, he said.
